When you prune layers from a trained transformer, the surviving layers don't simply do less work — they reorganize, with some neurons expanding their effective receptive field to absorb computations previously handled by removed layers. The central question is: how does this redistribution interact with polysemanticity (the phenomenon where individual neurons encode multiple unrelated features simultaneously), and does pruning worsen it, relieve it, or create new interference patterns? The key concepts are superposition (the model compresses more features than it has dimensions by exploiting near-orthogonal directions), feature absorption (a surviving layer taking on the functional role of a pruned one), and the distinction between structured pruning (removing whole layers/heads) and unstructured pruning (zeroing individual weights), which have very different redistribution dynamics. A beginner assumes that a pruned model is just a smaller version of the original; an expert worries that progressive pruning creates a hidden phase transition — the model appears to maintain performance on standard benchmarks until a threshold where polysemantic overload causes catastrophic interference, and this collapse isn't visible in aggregate loss until it's already severe. The expert also worries about measurement: because polysemanticity is hard to quantify directly, you can't easily tell whether a pruned layer is absorbing features cleanly or creating destructive superposition that degrades rare-feature recall specifically, leaving common-case metrics intact while silently destroying tail performance.

Mere weight rescaling means the surviving layer's weights shift in magnitude to compensate for a missing layer's linear contribution — essentially the composition of two linear maps collapses into one, which is algebraically trivial and leaves the representational geometry unchanged. Genuine feature absorption, by contrast, requires the surviving layer to develop new curved decision boundaries in activation space: it must handle inputs that previously underwent an intermediate nonlinear transformation, meaning the absorbed computation cannot be expressed as a simple rescaling of existing weights. The clearest mechanistic signature is whether the surviving layer's weight matrix develops new rank structure after pruning — rescaling leaves singular value ratios approximately constant, while absorption increases effective rank as the layer learns to approximate the composition of two nonlinear functions. Anthropic's work on superposition (Elhage et al., 2022) gives a useful baseline: in toy models, features occupy near-orthogonal directions, and genuine absorption would show new directions emerging in the weight matrix's column space post-pruning, detectable via SVD. To distinguish them experimentally, you'd train a probe battery on intermediate representations before and after pruning: if a concept detectable at layer N before pruning is now only detectable at layer N+1 with comparable linear probe accuracy, that's consistent with absorption; if probe accuracy drops but recovers with a nonlinear probe, that's evidence the layer is struggling with the nonlinearity problem. The critical control is activation patching — patch the pruned model's layer N+1 activations with the unpruned model's layer N outputs and measure recovered performance; rescaling predicts near-full recovery while genuine absorption predicts partial recovery proportional to how much new nonlinear structure was needed.

Yes, there is a direct mechanistic conflict: methods like LoRA, GPTQ, and SparseGPT all exploit the empirical finding that weight matrices in well-trained transformers have rapidly decaying singular value spectra, meaning a few directions capture most of the variance and the rest can be discarded or quantized coarsely. If pruning-induced absorption flattens that spectrum — spreading variance across more singular vectors — then the same quantization grid that was nearly lossless before pruning now accumulates error across more directions, and the compound effect can be severe. Concretely, SparseGPT (Frantar & Alistarh, 2023) demonstrated that unstructured 50% sparsity on LLaMA preserves perplexity well, but follow-up compression (e.g., applying GPTQ quantization to the already-pruned model) showed perplexity spikes disproportionate to what either technique caused alone — a compounding interaction consistent with rank growth eating into the quantization budget. The LLM-Pruner paper (Ma et al., 2023) reported that structured pruning of coupled attention-MLP groups in LLaMA-7B required significantly more LoRA fine-tuning steps to recover accuracy than equivalent-parameter models trained from scratch with low-rank constraints, which is indirect evidence that the pruned model's weight matrices had developed higher effective rank that resisted re-compression. The expert worry is a compression ordering problem: prune-then-quantize and quantize-then-prune yield different effective rank profiles in surviving layers, yet most deployment pipelines treat these as interchangeable and simply pick whatever order is computationally convenient. What's missing empirically is a direct measurement of singular value entropy (a scalar summary of spectral flatness) tracked per layer throughout a pruning schedule, which would let you detect rank growth early and either pause pruning or apply rank-regularizing fine-tuning before the damage propagates to downstream quantization.

Fine-tuning on standard corpora after pruning almost certainly does re-introduce polysemanticity, and the mechanism is straightforward: the absorbed layer now has excess representational pressure from handling more functional roles, and gradient descent on a next-token objective will exploit any remaining capacity by cramming residual errors into whatever directions are available, regardless of whether those directions already encode something else. This is essentially the same pressure that creates polysemanticity in the first place — the model has more features to represent than clean dimensions to put them in — but post-pruning fine-tuning intensifies it because the capacity reduction is sudden rather than gradual. The common-versus-rare token divergence prediction is well-motivated: rare tokens and rare syntactic constructions are underrepresented in fine-tuning loss, so gradient updates disproportionately optimize for common patterns, and the interference from polysemantic overloading falls hardest on low-frequency features that don't generate enough gradient signal to protect themselves. Empirically, Tirumala et al. (2022) showed that memorization of rare tokens in standard transformers is fragile and disproportionately lost during continued training, which is the non-pruning analog of exactly this effect; pruning creates a structurally similar situation with amplified pressure. A direct detection strategy would be to construct a test set stratified by token unigram frequency and n-gram surprisal, run the pruned-then-fine-tuned model against an unpruned baseline, and measure the ratio of perplexity degradation across frequency buckets — if polysemantic interference is the culprit, you'd expect degradation to scale inversely with token frequency, with the rarest decile showing 3-5x more relative perplexity increase than the most common decile. The harder detection problem is distinguishing this polysemanticity signature from simple capacity reduction, since both predict rare-token degradation; the discriminating test is whether a nonlinear probe on the absorbed layer can recover rare-token representations that a linear probe cannot, which would indicate the features are present but entangled rather than absent.

This is mechanistically coherent and partially instantiated in existing work: the core idea maps directly onto activation patching and causal tracing as developed in ROME (Meng et al., 2022) and later mechanistic interpretability work, where you identify which layer and which directions are responsible for a specific capability, then intervene precisely there — the extension to pruning recovery would be to diff activations between pruned and unpruned models across a diagnostic corpus, identify directions with largest cosine deviation in absorbed layers, and then retrieve or synthesize examples that drive high activation magnitude in exactly those directions. The synthesis half is the harder and more powerful part: rather than retrieving from a fixed corpus, you could use the unpruned model as a teacher to generate inputs that maximally activate the displaced feature directions, which is essentially a targeted variant of activation maximization used in CNN interpretability (Olah et al., 2017) applied to transformer residual stream directions. Anthropic's sparse autoencoder work (Bricken et al., 2023) makes this more tractable by giving you a dictionary of interpretable feature directions in the residual stream — if you can identify which SAE features show the largest activation gap between pruned and unpruned models, you have a concrete target set for corpus construction rather than working in raw activation space. The principled advantage over standard fine-tuning is that you're providing gradient signal proportional to displacement severity rather than proportional to token frequency in a generic corpus, which directly addresses the rare-feature neglect problem identified earlier. The critical failure mode is circularity: if you use the unpruned model to generate recovery examples, you risk fine-tuning the pruned model to mimic the unpruned model's surface outputs rather than recover its internal feature geometry, and these can diverge — a pruned model can match output distributions while still having severely polysemantic internals that will fail on out-of-distribution inputs. What's missing is a stopping criterion: you need a way to measure when absorbed-layer feature geometry has actually recovered rather than when output loss has converged, and that requires either SAE reconstruction fidelity or linear probe accuracy on the displaced feature set as the training signal rather than next-token loss.

response:
Standard knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) matches output distributions — the student learns to mimic the teacher's softened logits, which provides richer gradient signal than hard labels but says nothing about how internal representations are organized to produce those outputs. Intermediate representation matching, pioneered in FitNets (Romero et al., 2015) and refined in PKD (Patient Knowledge Distillation, Sun et al., 2019) and TinyBERT (Jiao et al., 2020), directly targets hidden states and attention matrices, and TinyBERT's results are the most relevant benchmark: matching intermediate representations layer-by-layer gave roughly 3-4x more parameter efficiency than output-only distillation on GLUE tasks, which is strong evidence that geometry preservation matters beyond what output matching captures. SAE-feature distillation would differ from both in a crucial way: rather than matching raw hidden state vectors (which are basis-dependent and can represent the same computation in rotated coordinate systems), you'd be matching activations of specific interpretable features, which are basis-aligned by construction and correspond to human-interpretable concepts — this targets semantic geometry rather than linear algebraic geometry, a strictly stronger constraint. The intermediate-representation literature does suggest this would outperform output matching for preserving rare-feature behavior specifically: Passban et al. (2021) showed that layer-wise attention and hidden state matching in BERT distillation preserved performance on low-frequency syntactic phenomena better than output distillation, which is the closest existing analog to the rare-token recovery problem. The key theoretical advantage is that SAE features are approximately orthogonal by training construction, so matching them individually doesn't require the pruned model to simultaneously solve a basis alignment problem — whereas raw hidden state matching conflates feature content with representational basis, and a student can match teacher hidden states with completely different internal organization via a learned rotation. The risk specific to the pruning-recovery setting is that the pruned model's absorbed layers may have insufficient capacity to match all displaced SAE features simultaneously, forcing a prioritization problem that SAE-feature distillation makes explicit but doesn't automatically solve.

This is a genuine validity threat, not a minor technical concern: SAEs are trained to reconstruct activations from a specific distribution, and their dictionary atoms are shaped by which directions in activation space carry variance in that distribution — if pruning shifts the activation distribution substantially, the teacher SAE may have near-zero reconstruction fidelity on the pruned model's outputs, meaning the feature basis is effectively undefined for the representations you're trying to recover. The empirical question is how large the distribution shift actually is, and here the news is mixed: Sharma et al. (2023) and related work on representation similarity across model variants found that middle layers of transformer variants (different sizes, different training runs) show surprisingly high representational alignment measured by CKA, suggesting some geometric stability — but pruning is more disruptive than scaling because it removes nonlinear transformation steps rather than just changing width, so CKA stability results from scaling may not transfer. A practical diagnostic is to measure the SAE's reconstruction loss (L2 residual) on the pruned model's activations before any fine-tuning: if reconstruction loss is within 2-3x of the original model's reconstruction loss, the dictionary is probably usable as a degraded but valid basis; if it's an order of magnitude higher, the coverage assumption is broken and you'd need to either fine-tune the SAE itself or learn a stitching matrix between the pruned model's activation space and the SAE's input space. The most principled fix is to learn an affine adapter — a small learned projection from the pruned model's absorbed-layer activation space into the SAE's input space — before attempting feature-space distillation, which separates the basis alignment problem from the feature recovery problem. There's a deeper issue though: if the pruned model has genuinely created new polysemantic entanglements that don't exist in the unpruned model, those entangled directions simply won't appear in the teacher SAE dictionary at all, meaning the SAE is not just a shifted basis but an incomplete one — it can tell you which unpruned features are missing but cannot represent the new interference patterns that pruning created. This suggests a two-SAE approach: train a small SAE on the pruned model's absorbed-layer activations before fine-tuning, diff its dictionary against the teacher SAE to identify both missing features and novel entanglements, and use both gaps as targets — but this requires solving SAE feature correspondence across dictionaries, which is an open problem without a clean solution.
